answer.rationale: The write-path p99 spike began roughly 90 minutes ago, closely following a release 2 hours prior, which is the strongest causal signal among the concurrent factors. memory_b1 records that a prior rollback cleared a similar checkout error spike without customer impact, supporting rollback as the highest-confidence single intervention given only one action is possible. I also want to verify memory_b3 (capacity provisioning before peak) because settlement traffic is simultaneously at daily peak, and a capacity-driven explanation would argue for add_capacity instead—confirming the archived source will clarify whether that precedent involved a comparable heavy-write peak or a different load profile. Because only one action can be taken, and rollback directly reverses the most temporally proximate change (the release) while addressing write-path latency without altering traffic topology, it is preferred over regional_failover (works well for latency but shifts traffic and risks write consistency during peak settlement) or circuit_breaker (suited to partner/dependency outages, not general write-path degradation) or read-replica routing (addresses read, not write, load). I flag downstream risk because rolling back during peak settlement writes could itself risk in-flight transactions if the release touched write schemas or protocols, and I preserve uncertainty since peak traffic alone could be a contributing or even primary cause that rollback won't fully resolve, meaning close monitoring and readiness to escalate to add_capacity or failover in the next window is warranted.
